speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In light of this morning's report on the study compiled by MOT into the violations of aviation rules in Canada, and in particular northwestern Ontario; and in light of the statements made by the minister that after conducting an internal inquiry into flying procedures in northern Ontario he would launch a public inquiry, if warranted, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski):
That this House urge the Minister of Transport to honour his commitment and immediately call a public inquiry into the conditions under which aircraft operate in Canada in general and in northwestern Ontario in particular.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SOLICITOR GENERAL BE RESPONSIBLE FOR OPERATING POLICY OF SECURITY SERVICE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Last week the Solicitor General announced a number of administrative changes within the upper echelons of the security service force to ensure greater control over security activities. This new administrative structure is seriously deficient, however, in that it makes no specific provision for the Solicitor General to provide policy direction or input into the operational policy committee. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence):
That this House requests that the Solicitor General consider revising or enlarging the structure of the operational policy committee to provide direct consultation between the committee and the Solicitor General; and that this House further directs that this committee hold frequent and meaningful meetings so that the Solicitor General is made both responsible and accountable for the operating policy of the security service.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT SAFETY REGULATIONS BE MORE STRICTLY ENFORCED-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Given the allegations made by two investigators for the Department of Transport that aviation safety across Canada, and particularly in northwestern Ontario, is being jeopardized by the department's failure to adequately enforce air regulations and take action against companies and individuals routinely engaged in illegal and dangerous air practice, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles);
That this House urges the Minister of Transport to immediately stop the situation in which senior officials of his department are effectively stopping attempts of regional safety officers from applying disciplinary action in order to enforce safety regulations; and furthermore, urges the minister to stop the current practice in which aviation firms and individuals in the north break the law and endanger the lives of employees and passengers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The persistent perennial ice conditions will again face Newfoundland fishermen and shipping to northern Newfoundland in the months from December to March, and past experience shows clearly that icebreaker vessels in Halifax are too distant to provide the service required, causing hindrance and loss of income to fishermen. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse):
That the government give immediate consideration to the deployment of icebreaking vessels to Newfoundland during the months indicated, and further, that any new vessels in work be designated for that province.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED PROHIBITION OF PROPOSED ELIMINATION OF EXPRESS SERVICE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas it is the intention of the CNR to gradually eliminate its express service as demonstrated by the lay-off of 360 employees in that department in the next few weeks, and the probable lay-off of hundreds more in the next couple of years, and whereas this decision will mean not only unemployment but that the goods which until now had been moved by the fuel efficient railways, will in the future be moved by air or truck which will use substantially more of our scarce oil and gas I therefore move:
That this House urges the CNR to stop its planned elimination of its express department.

speechtext: The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar wishes to raise a point of order, and I have notice of a question of privilege from the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton on the same subject.

speechtext:

Ministerial Responsibility

The reason this becomes even more of a pressing issue in this case is that the acting minister designated by order in council has been going around, outside the House of Commons, making statements which have the effect of smearing the RCMP and every officer and constable in that force.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: He is not merely a member of the cabinet; he is the Acting Solicitor General who makes such statements, and when the opportunity arises for us to ask him questions with respect to his statements outside the House which create damage to the force and to which we take particular exception, he refuses to answer. Arrogance.
Shame.

speechtext: I have heard the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, and I will now hear the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton on whether there is any obligation attached to the arrangement respecting acting ministers. prepared to answer questions with respect to a certain matter unless it was within his present responsibilities.
Now, sir, the questions today were put to the Acting Solicitor General within his existing responsibilities as Acting Solicitor General-not to any other member on the front bench designated by any whim or last-minute decision, but in accordance with order in council No. 1977-2865 passed on October 6, 1977. Just so you will understand the situation, Mr. Speaker- I do not know whether you have had a chance to see it-let me say that under the section dealing with the Solicitor General we see that the minister is shown as being Francis Fox, and the acting minister is shown as being Warren Allmand. The second acting minister, I presume to act in the absence of the first acting minister, is shown as being Stanley Ronald Basford.
What happened in the House of Commons today was that questions were put by two members of the House, the right hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot, to the Acting Solicitor General. In his present capacity, under the order in council of Acting Solicitor General, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs-without looking up-made a gesture, pointing to the Minister of Justice. I do not care what he does with his finger, Mr. Speaker, but it is quite important what happens in terms of the responsibility of ministers of the Crown to answer questions. The fact is that the designation of the minister on any day is not whimsical; there has been a studied effort by the government to designate acting ministers to be accountable, to use your words, Mr. Speaker, for their present capacity.
By that order in council, the present capacity of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is with respect to the work of his particular department and also with respect to the functions of the Solicitor General in the absence of the Solicitor General. So we put questions to the Acting Solicitor General in his capacity as Acting Solicitor General. Quite frankly, I think that if the question period is to mean anything, we cannot be prevented from asking the Acting Solicitor General questions relating to his capacity as Acting Solicitor General-and if we are, this would be the third line drawn on our privileges. That point seems to be important.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is misstating what I said. The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar indicated that had the questions been answered today, or had the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs answered questions in his capacity as Acting Solicitor General today, he could have been asked questions about his capacity as a former solicitor general. That is the distinction I make.
When he rises to answer in his capacity as Acting Solicitor General he is responsible, equally with the present Solicitor General, for actions in that department for all time, and questions which would have been proper to ask the present Solicitor General about events under previous solicitors general would have been quite proper, but they would have been faced with precisely the same conditions and limitations. None
November 28, 1977

differ. Any minister in an acting minister's capacity represents that minister as fully as he possibly can in the circumstances. There is no distinction there. But the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar was attempting, it seems to me, to indicate that he might have been able to ask questions which were otherwise prohibited, and I think that would not be the case.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I gather the situation is that, even though a minister of the Crown who just happened to be solicitor general at one point and who is now filling in for the Solicitor General could answer all kinds of questions about a prior solicitor general, the person who is the Acting Solicitor General today is limited with respect to his powers and the responsibility he has in an acting capacity, and therefore is not bound to answer. Just so that we understand completely what Your Honour is saying, by juggling acting ministers the ministry has effectively limited the right of the opposition to ask questions about the capacity of a minister who was a full minister in a former capacity and who is now only an acting minister in that capacity.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let me put it in a positive way so that the record will be clear. Questions which are proper to be put to a minister are the same questions which are proper to be put under all the same conditions to a minister who is acting in that person's stead. It is as simple as that. There is no problem with that. The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar put forward a proposition that questions which would have been improper on a previous occasion might have been proper. In any case, whether that was his argument or not, he raised questions about that matter.
To clarify that aspect, questions which would be proper to the present Solicitor General would be proper to another minister acting in his stead. What I am not persuaded of is the basis of the point of order and the question of privilege, which is that there is some binding validity, in a procedural sense, on the Chair with respect to the designation of acting ministers. It is a new point: I have never heard it argued before, and I am prepared to examine the precedents and hear arguments from both sides on it. But that is the basis of the point of order and the question of privilege as I understand it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief comment to make on the very narrow point of order which has been raised. Hon. members are acting under the assumption that the Minister of Justice answered those questions in the capacity of Acting Solicitor General. It is my view that the minister answered those questions pertaining to a lawsuit to which he is a party, in his capacity as Minister of Justice, and he is fully entitled to do so. Therefore, the point of order at this point is without foundation.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am still a little confused on one point. If I had put the question to the present Solicitor General, "Will you get the consent of the two former solicitors general to come before the Standing
Ministerial Responsibility
Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs?", surely that would have been a proper question. If I had put a question to the Acting Solicitor General, he would have been in a dual capacity but he would have been acting as the Solicitor General. It is true he would have had knowledge of the past, but as I could ask questions about the past of the Solicitor General, I do not think we should be denied the right to ask the Acting Solicitor General. That is the point I am making. Surely, if the Solicitor General was asked a simple question-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Calgary North is pursuing an argument which has been raised by two other members previously. I also participated. However, let us bear in mind that I have attempted to put it as clearly as I possibly can. The conditions under which questions can be put to ministers are precisely the same conditions under which questions can be put to their acting ministers. I do not think I can make it any clearer than that.
Besides that, any argument about what questions could or could not be put to an acting minister are academic to the point raised, because they were never put. The point raised today is whether there is a requirement upon the ministry to put forward the acting minister who is designated by some order as the person to answer questions if a question is directed to the Acting Solicitor General, as was the case today. That is the point at issue. That is the point on which there has been argument from the government side, that questions were not answered in that capacity. More central to the argument, it seems to me, is that if there is no obligation on a minister to answer a question at any time, how can there be an obligation on an acting minister? It seems to me that that is the point I have to sort out: that is the point which is basic.
The other argument is one in which we were involved. Perhaps the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar and I were talking at cross-purposes, but it remains an academic problem because it did not take place.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could make one other point. When the Deputy Prime Minister said that the questions were asked of the Minister of Justice in his capacity as Minister of Justice, it is true he was involved in that lawsuit; it is true he was involved in the motion. But the questions were put by distinguished and honourable members to the Acting Solicitor General. That was the minister we wanted to ask, that is the minister we wanted to answer, and the argument put forward by the Deputy Prime Minister was another red herring to hide the truth.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I say, again, that the point has two fundamental aspects. First, is there, by virtue of an order designating acting ministers, an obligation which binds us, in the sense of our procedures, to carry that through the question period in the sense which was argued today? Second, if there cannot be an obligation upon a minister to answer a question during the question period, can I Find one on an acting minister? I do not know. I have to examine those aspects to see whether I can give any validity to the arguments put forward.
80027-13V4

Ministerial Responsibility

Mr. Speaker, may I say a word further on the narrow point of order as you have so described it? I do so to express the hope that Your Honour will come back with a ruling. If a minister is in the House, none of us would be permitted to ask the acting minister a question; we would be told that the minister is here. I think that, by the same token, if the first acting minister is here and the minister is not, it should not be possible to jump down to the second acting minister. The ex post facto explanation the President of the Privy Council has given us is a very interesting one which is worth studying, but I think on the main point raised there should be a ruling that if a minister is present, he is asked the questions-

-but if the first acting minister is here, he should be asked the questions, not the second acting minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may, occasionally through inadvertence members misdirect questions and the minister who exercises responsibility for the subject matter rises even though the questions are addressed to another minister. That happens occasionally.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not the case here.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: However, in this case it seems to me that the onus is on the other side. Perhaps hon. members opposite think they ought to decide who should answer for the government in every particular case, regardless of responsibility; but the fact of the matter is that in reply to the question put by the right hon. gentleman, the Minister of Justice answered, in my view, within his capacity as Minister of Justice-
Why didn't you say so at the time?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -because both ministers are parties to the lawsuit. And who is to say-unless it be by some fiat from the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton-that it must be the Solicitor General? Or does he argue that there ought to be a duet and both ought to answer simultaneously? Unless he argues that, either minister is free to answer. I argue that the point of order is really quite theological and more appropriate for theologians than politicians.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I always knew that the hon. Deputy Prime Minister brought great dignity to our proceedings, but dignity beyond ours is new. I will recognize the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar as I allowed the Deputy Prime Minister a second intervention.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address myself briefly to two points. The Deputy Prime Minister entered this debate and indicated that the questions were directed to the government and could be answered by the Minister of Justice.
I think Your Honour should bear in mind that there is a real

problem to face here. The questions put by the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot dealt with the structure of the overview committee on security services, and I would be very surprised if the Minister of Justice could weasle his way into that answer. It was, clearly, a question specifically about the structure announced by the Solicitor General and had nothing to do with the Minister of Justice, even in the broadest theological debate that I could think of.
After dismissing that specious argument on the part of the Deputy Minister, I want to make it abundantly clear-and we may have been at cross-purposes here-that it was not my intention to suggest that a question that otherwise might have been improper could have been asked of an acting minister. I am sorry if I was not as clear as I should have been. The point I was making was that when we have an acting minister, he is the person from whom we ought to hear on questions dealing with departmental responsibility, particularly when they deal with events which happened in that department while he was minister.
When he subsequently appears outside the House and smears the RCMP by suggesting that they have been misleading him, or were coming forward with false information or withholding information, then it becomes particularly important for us to deal with the acting minister, because he not only has the responsibility by order in council but has particular and peculiar knowledge which would enlighten the people of Canada on his reasons for taking the rather unfortunate step of smearing the RCMP.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not in the House. She, either deliberately or unwittingly-and I suspect the latter-misled the House today in reply to a supplementary question which I directed to her. During the course of my question I commended what I call, and I support, the commendable objectives of the minister in broadening the scope of a floor income for Canadians by having a limited
November 28, 1977

sector of those who are drawing certain benefits rationalized into some form of guaranteed annual income.
In the course of the question I asked the minister if she was now prepared to eliminate the discriminatory provisions of the Canada Pension Plan which discriminate against housewives or those who stay at home to look after families. They do not enjoy equal rights under the Canada Pension Plan, which does not recognize the occupation of homemaker for contributions or benefits. In her reply, the minister tried to convey to the House the view that this matter had been dealt with by legislation during the latter part of the last session. It is a fact that some amendments to the Canada Pension Plan were brought in during the latter part of the last session, but this was not one of them. They did not deal with this discriminatory provision of the Canada Pension Plan, and I believe the minister should correct that misleading statement at the first opportunity.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as Acting Minister of National Health and Welfare, may I point out to the hon. member that there is no discrimination in those provisions. That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
speechtext: You have to earn a salary, wages or income in order to be eligible to pay contributions to the Canada Pension Plan. Regarding my hon. colleague's answer to the hon. member, she pointed out that some amendments were made least year to provide for the splitting of credit between spouses at the time of divorce or marriage breakdown. I am sure that is what she meant when she referred to this particular situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am sure the hon. minister did not intentionally mislead the House. There seems to be a variety of interpretations of what she said or intended to say, and I am sure the minister will take the first opportunity to clarify what she said.

speechtext: The hon. member for York-Simcoe, on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, when we were dealing with clause 1 on Friday I raised the question of what, in fact, was the relative increase with and without indexing in income tax in relation to the general increase of income itself. At that time the minister stated, as reported at page 1257 of Hansard:
-this is a highly technical question, and I am not in a position to answer it right now. I will get the information and forward it to the hon. member later today.
Subsequently, the minister indicated that he would put on the record of this House exactly what is that relative ratio between income tax and the general increase of personal income both before and after indexing. 1 was just wondering if the Minister of Finance could be given a chance now to put it on the record.

Mr. Chairman, I have here a technical answer to a technical problem, so perhaps I could try to read it. However, it is not in the form of a reply and I will have to

adjust accordingly. I am advised by my officials that the same question has been put to my predecessor, as well, on numerous occasions. The hon. member for York-Simcoe has been made aware on these occasions that it is difficult to summarize the responsiveness of federal revenues in terms of one single number, sometimes called "elasticity". For his benefit, let me explain the technical aspects of this concept one more time.
The total growth in income in any given year is composed of three components. These are the growth in the number of taxpayers, the growth in productivity or real per capita income, and the growth in prices. The response of revenues to each of these factors is different. The growth in the number of tax filers has approximately proportional effect on revenues. A 1 per cent growth in real per capita income increases revenues by approximately 1.7 per cent to 1.8 per cent. In the absence of indexing, a 1 per cent growth in prices has the same effect as a 1 per cent growth in real income. However, indexing ensures that the inflation-related growth in income has a proportional effect on revenues. In other words, with indexing, if prices increase by 1 per cent, nominal revenues also increase by the same 1 per cent, thereby leaving the real value of taxes unchanged.
The over-all response of the personal income tax revenues to growth in income is a weighted average of the three factors I have just identified. I indicated in my fiscal statement of October 20 that in a typical year, with 2 per cent growth in productivity, the over-all elasticity of revenues would be about 1.3. This is, of course, variable over time and sensitive to the cyclical state of the economy. Moreover, this elasticity is affected by any new tax changes proposed in a given year.

On a point of clarification, Mr. Chairman, the minister has indicated, or at least created the impression, that this point has been raised several times and he will answer it once again-or has been given a written statement from his officials with a view to answering it. Is it not true that this is the first time this question has ever been asked? Any other time it has been raised, it has not been raised in this House but in an in camera session.

I am not in a position to give any more explanation. I was not the minister at that time. The hon. member said this question was debated before. I do not know whether it was here, or elsewhere, in camera. With the new minister, he is right in the open.

speechtext: Order. The Minister of Finance on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I object to the remarks of the hon. member. I never said: What's a billion! He is the one who said that and it is obviously a very arrogant attitude from a former finance minister of Newfoundland who did not have very often the opportunity of seeing $1 billion during the time he was in office.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance is becoming very sensitive. I can understand why. He has already made thousands of mistakes in his short tenure as Minister of Finance. He cannot make too many more that will not be recognized. I agree he did not say, "What's a billion". He positively did not. In 1976, the figures would be roughly the same. There were 8.8 million taxable returns filed, and $17'/2 billion collected in personal income tax. Therefore, we are dealing with serious business.
I suggest to this committee that this bill should not pass until the Canadian public is assured on three matters. The first deals with the matter of the confidentiality of income tax returns that are filed. That is a matter that came up in the House about a week ago. We still do not have any report from the Minister of National Revenue or the Minister of Finance as to whether income tax returns are privileged and confidential information, or whether we can phone the Ministry of National Revenue and get the information. As far as we know now, income tax returns are not confidential. Anyone with an inquiring mind who wants to know what our returns are can telephone the department and get the information or press a computer button to get it. In any event, they get the information.
There has been no statement since this information came out a week ago. The Minister of National Revenue should be here before the committee ready to answer for his responsibility to the 8.8 million taxpayers of Canada as to whether that information is available to the public, or not, or what he is doing to prevent that situation. That is one area, Mr. Chairman.

At this time I have to report that the matter is under investigation by the RCMP. Apparently, there was one individual who had a way of obtaining information he should not have had. As soon as the inquiry is completed, he will be penalized according to the laws of the land, because the taxpayers of Canada are to be protected in the confidentiality of their returns.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I suggest that the hon. member for St. John's West keep his remarks quite general. As these clauses come up, he can put his arguments.

Mr. Chairman, I submit that was not a point of order. The time should not come out of the time that I have before the committee. This clause deals with collecting tax from the people of Canada. I am speaking on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada who are going to suffer or gain under this clause. Their suffering or gain may become public knowledge if the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance do not take the steps necessary to stop the leaking of confidential information to anyone who might want it. That must be clarified before the bill leaves the committee.
The second point that must also be made clear relates as well, to income tax. That is the reports of violations of the law in connection with income tax collection, secret tax information given by National Revenue to the RCMP and municipal police forces across Canada, as reported in the press in recent weeks. In fact, employees of the Department of National Revenue who collected the income tax we are dealing with now have perjured themselves before the courts in that connection.
I refer in particular to the matter that came before the Laycraft inquiry and the listening devices, interception of telephone messages, wiretaps and the like. That kind of procedure has been used to gather information on income tax. It is forbidden to be done in that manner by collusion and co-operation between the RCMP and the Department of National Revenue. Before this committee authorizes the government to collect any income tax under the provisions of this bill, that situation should be clarified. It is the Income Tax Act that we are now amending.
Is it correct, as Mr. Morris Bradshaw told the Laycraft inquiry, that the practice of releasing tax information on certain Canadians preceded the 1972 agreement between the Department of the MNR and the RCMP which formalized that procedure, and that confidential tax information is released to police departments across Canada on anyone the Department of National Revenue wants investigated. That is the evidence that has been given to the Laycraft inquiry by officials of the Department of National Revenue. Is it correct? The agreement of 1972 was only supposed to relate to information dealing with organized crime. However, this MNR official said that this kind of information goes to police departments all across Canada whenever the Department of National Revenue wants to let it out. It is given out routinely.
If the members of this committee are to take their duty seriously, we have to get some explanation as to whether this is so, or not, as reported in the daily press. It has been made
Income Tax
quite clear that the Department of National Revenue and the municipal police forces-and I am referring to the Globe and Mail who quoted Mr. Bradshaw and his evidence at the inquiry-worked outside the agreement. Mr. Bradshaw was asked, "It has nothing to do with organized crime?" He answered, "Correct".
The RCMP have already given evidence that they are co-operating with National Revenue, that they use wiretap devices under the procedure of subterfuge, and that they exchange information gathered by wiretap with the Department of National Revenue although it is illegal to use wiretaps during an investigation into tax violations. An official of the minister's department, one Edmund Swartzack, was given transcripts of conversations by the RCMP. This was admitted. Inspector Graham George said that when the RCMP know they cannot wiretap under the Income Tax Act, they look for a Criminal Code violation and the information gathered is used for income tax purposes. That is complete and utter disregard for the laws of this country.
Are we supposed to sit in this committee and pass a bill which gives the crowd opposite the power to borrow $9 billion to continue to allow illegal activity in the collection of income tax across Canada? I say "no". Before the committee passes this bill there should be some satisfactory reply by ministers to these statements, and sworn evidence before inquiries.
Apparently, Mr. Edmund Swartzack-I do not know the gentleman-testified before the Federal Court and denied that the RCMP and the Department of National Revenue were working together in the summer of 1975 investigating the Royal American Shows. He told the court under oath that they were not working together. He denied the RCMP had given him information to help him in his investigation into income tax offences. He denied that before the end of May, 1975, he met RCMP officers engaged in investigating the company. In September he told the Laycraft inquiry that those answers had been untrue. He said he had not properly understood the question put to him and that his memory had failed him. Imagine an official saying that, when he was asked those simple questions, he had not understood them! Therefore, he admitted that he gave false testimony before the Federal Court in that area.
When are we going to get an explanation from the Minister of National Revenue as to what is going on in his department? Are his officials allowed to give evidence before the Federal Court in one direction, and before a royal commission to the contrary with such a weak and feeble excuse? Are the RCMP and his department working together contrary to the statutes of this country in these matters? That is the second area where I submit we need to have a full explanation and full disclosure by the government before we pass this bill.
The third area is whether the Income Tax Act is being administered impartially or whether certain taxpayers, one in particular, have been favoured ahead of all other taxpayers in this country. This is a question which should be answered. I am about to suggest that we need an immediate royal commission of inquiry into the favourable tax treatment accorded to a

certain individual whom I shall be mentioning in a few moments.
If more than eight million Canadians are obliged by law to pay income tax, if they are obliged to pay it on time, and if, should they dispute the amount of this tax, they are required to pay the amount of the tax first or else put up security in the form of bank guarantees and bonds-in most cases securities are not accepted; they have to pay up-why should the law be different in the case of one of them? This is something I want to have cleared up before this legislation leaves the committee.
I am referring to the case of one, John Christopher Doyle. If I was dealing with the case of a loyal Canadian, a man we could all admire and seek to emulate, I would concede there might be some reason to overlook the situation. But when one realizes that a certain Canadian taxpayer has been allowed to owe the government millions of dollars since 1950, that he still has not paid one cent of the money he owes, and that he has received preferential treatment beyond the belief of anybody in this chamber, it is an entirely different matter and one which demands explanation.
On June 11, 1959, John Christopher Doyle, the man who has been in control of Canadian Javelin Limited since its inception, was reassessed for income tax owing for 1950 and 1954. The reassessment involved a total of something like $900,000 for those two years, and was dated June 11, 1959. The gentleman in question appealed to the Income Tax Appeal Board. Here is the first area which demands explanation. The appeal was not heard until eight years later. Remember, the gentleman in question was not forced to pay his income tax. He was not forced to pay interest. As far as I can learn, he was not forced to put up any security. It was not until 1967 that the Income Tax Appeal Board heard his appeal. The board heard his appeal in each case, dismissed them and confirmed that he had been properly reassessed, with small adjustments, in relation to those two tax years 1950 and 1954.
Surely, the normal amount of time which elapses between an assessment and the hearing of appeal is not eight years. That is one matter which calls for investigation. Following that, the decision of the Income Tax Appeal Board was taken before the Exchequer Court of Canada. It took three years for that case to be heard. Because of the way in which the courts are run, perhaps three years' delay is not unknown. Anyway, in 1970 the case was heard before Mr. Justice Gibson in the Exchequer Court and he gave a judgment in June, 1970, reconfirming the reassessments for the tax years 1950 and 1954. That was in 1970, 20 years after the first tax year in question; that is, 1950, and 16 years after the second. So it is obvious the Crown was not pushing this matter forward; it was not doing everything possible to get the issue settled. One might have thought that 20 years after the reassessment the Crown would have said, "By gosh, it is time we got our hands on these millions which are owed to us by this taxpayer- particularly in view of the fact that he is a character who is not desirable in any event."

Notice of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada was entered by Mr. Doyle in October, 1970. Was the case heard in 1971? It was not. Was the case heard in 1972? It was not. Was the case heard in 1973? No. Was the case heard in 1974? No. Was the case heard in 1975? No. Was the case heard in 1976? No. Finally, one of the appeals was heard in October, 1977, and then only because I had raised the matter in the House on two or three occasions and complained-and I intend to bring it up on every occasion I can until the whole thing has been settled or some satisfactory explanation is given.
Seven years after those judgments were handed down by the Exchequer Court of Canada, one of the cases came before the Supreme Court-the case relating to the year 1950. The court dismissed the appeal from the bench; the judges did not even reserve judgment so that they could hand it down in writing. It was clear that the taxpayer had no case. Yet it took the Canadian government 27 years to get the matter before the Supreme Court. What does this mean? What is the explanation? I shall come to the explanation a little later in my remarks. It is a tawdry one, a political one, a scandalous one. I might add that the other case, the case involving 1954, has not yet been heard by the Supreme Court, but the Minister of Justice has assured me it will be heard this winter. The present Minister of Justice has been pushing this matter since I got on his tail, and he has promised me he will expedite it; it is getting some attention now. Anyway, it has taken 27 years to get the matter to its present stage.
If the taxpayer had been obliged to pay his tax, with interest-as is the normal course of events- it might be easier to look upon this 27-year process with a kinder eye. But he has not been required to pay the tax, and in the meantime he has become a fugitive from Justice in Canada. He has not lived here since the beginning of 1974, though he lived here from 1950 until that year. He became a fugitive from justice in the United States in 1965. He left that country because he had been sentenced in connection with a mail fraud-sending stock certificates through the mail-and he was ordered to serve three months of a three-year sentence. In addition, a fine was imposed. He left the United States and did not go back. He has been a fugitive from justice down there since 1965. The government knew this, yet it persisted in its negligence.
In December of 1973 he was charged in Canada with acts of criminal fraud and breach of trust in Newfoundland. Since then, 406 counts have been brought against him involving wash-trading. And where is he? He is down in Panama, Mr. Speaker. He got out on bail in December of 1973 and disappeared to Panama where he is now living very happily, continuing his operations, taking all the revenue out of Canadian Javelin Limited, a Canadian company incorporated under the federal Canada Corporations Act, so that the shareholders in that company are receiving nothing-nil, zero, zilch! Not a cent! They get no dividends. Nothing! It all goes out in various ways to Mr. John C. Doyle and his companions.
That is the kind of gentleman who was given this tender treatment, Mr. Speaker. What is the explanation? I put a
November 28, 1977

question on the order paper, and the answer I received reveals massive negligence on the part of the government of Canada, malfeasance, non-feasance-is that the right term to describe the process of deliberately doing nothing? There is non-feasance as well as malfeasance, procrastination and political pollution involved in this situation.
How about Pickersgill?

In answer to my question No. 1749 of last year, the government admitted it had received no moneys from Mr. John C. Doyle as a result of these judgments related to his appeals from assessment. However, the Crown states that it did take action to secure its claim. Then the answer goes on to say, and I quote:
It should be noted that as a result of a decline in the market value of the security held, the Crown's claim is now only partly secured.
The Crown has a lien on shares owned by John C. Doyle in Canadian Javelin Limited. As far as I know, they do not have the shares. They claim they have 125,000 of them, but they have a lien. If the shares are ever transferred, presumably the transfer agent has to deliver the shares to the Crown.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired, and I allowed a couple of extra minutes because of the intervention by the Minister of Finance.
I will come back to this, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this matter. I would agree with the increase from $1,000 to $2,000, but this really is only recognition of the fact that inflation is a serious problem which we are not taking into account when we are putting together our accounting figures. This will not be too onerous for the government, and it is not going to lose too much money. It is almost impossible for it to lose money now on the capital account, with the inflation we are experiencing. In effect, it is giving something that is not going to cost anything, or very little. I would ask the minister, when he has the opportunity to reply, why there will be no deductions if the taxpayer is a corporation. It seems to me that for small corporations such as a family farm or similar corporation there is situation here that is being overlooked. I would like to know whether, when the taxpayer is a corporation, small or large, he is entitled to make a deduction for capital loss.
In our accounting and tax practices we are not taking into account the enormous inflationary times we are experiencing. Profit and loss calculated according to accepted accounting principles are now so inaccurate as to be misleading. The present rules are hopelessly obsolete. This is very important because business in Canada, knowing that real profit is too low, slows down investment and thus employment. Labour, on the other hand, seeing reported profit as being too high, demands non-competitive wages, and consumers, believing profit to be the main factor in price rises, demand arbitrary controls imposed by politicians seeking re-election. All I am
Income Tax
saying is that profit is often badly overstated and the true corporate income tax rate is far higher than the stated rate, as well as corporate losses. This creates in the tax structure an imbalance we are only now recognizing.
It is interesting to note that the Ontario government created a committee to study and report on inflation accounting. It reported something quite interesting in that net return on investment in 1975 was 8.5 per cent, whereas in 1971 it was 5.75 per cent. When adjustment was made for inflation, the net return on investment was 2 per cent for 1975 and 2.5 per cent for 1971. So, in fact, while there was more profit in dollars in 1975 than in 1971, when the adjustment for inflation is made there is actually less return on investment. In fact, financial statements on certified professional accountants as presenting a true and accurate review of financial results are often so inaccurate as to be totally misleading. The importance of this is that our economic decisions have to be based on true competitive values exchanged or expected to be exchanged. It is of crucial importance, if financial data is to be used in investment, wages, buying or taxing decisions, that it be expressed in terms of real values.
The increase from $1,000 to $2,000 is, I suppose, a very crude way of assessing inflation, but it really does not get at the problem in relation to true inflation accounting. This presents a difficulty. But if we do not adjust financial data to reflect the real effect of inflation, all sectors will inevitably make wrong economic decisions. It is this situation that has forced Canada into the impending economic crisis.
I support this clause, but I might add that it is not going to cost the government very much. It is very difficult to have capital losses, given the inflation rate that is on paper. I believe this is only a beginning of what we have to study much more carefully in order to bring something to the tax system that recognizes the difficulty, and I have in mind inflation accounting.

I would like to ask the minister, in view of the fact that this particular problem results in many Canadians, some of them

senior citizens over the age of 80 or 90, and some parents having to take out social insurance numbers for young children three and four years old who have Canada Savings Bonds in their names, is the minister prepared to consider withdrawing that directive requiring the use of social insurance numbers for cashing Canada Savings Bonds interest coupons?

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might ask one further question. There is growing concern in the country because of the threat of misuse of social insurance numbers. In 1972, the government's very excellent study on privacy and computers recommended that the social insurance number not be used either in a legislative sense or in a de facto sense as a single identification number for citizens, but the increasing use of the social insurance number in various government programs as an identification number and as a computing coding number causes considerable problems.
This causes problems not just from a psychological point of view but also from the point of view of privacy, because if it is possible to get one's hands on a person's social insurance number that increases the possibility of getting access to information held in government files about that person. I refer the minister particularly to incidents which took place a couple of weeks ago when the disclosure was made that it was possible to get from the tax department information about the confidential and personal tax returns of individual Canadians.
I am wondering whether the minister would be prepared to consider amending Bill C-11 at the present time or to bring in amendments at another time which would disallow the use of social insurance numbers on tax forms. As the minister knows, it is possible to file an income tax form using either a tax filing number or a social insurance number, and I wonder whether to confine the use of the social insurance number strictly to the purpose for which it was designed the minister would be prepared to amend the act to remove the use of it on income tax forms?

Mr. Chairman, this is a controversy which is taking place at this time. I am informed that since 1966 taxpayers have been asked to put their social insurance number on their income tax returns, and that producing a social insurance number when cashing coupons is a new requirement brought about last summer after introduction by my predecessor, the hon. member for Rosedale. I was quite taken by the argument made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain and the hon. member for Edmonton West who said there was a commitment that social insurance numbers would never be used for this purpose. security number when cashing coupons is new. I have much sympathy for older and younger people, but according to the studies of my department there is a certain number of people cashing coupons. It is that when cashing coupons in any institution, the tax will be collected there and then. In this country we only impose this obligation on people who do not have a social insurance number. People who have a number do not pay the tax then, and the problem of collecting and repaying the tax is avoided. I am preoccupied with the problem of people who do not have a social insurance number, and am looking for alternatives. I would like to explore any suggestions that hon. members may make.

Parliament has passed legislation amending the Canada Pension Plan Act exempting certain religious groups from having to take social insurance numbers for conscientious reasons. My other point is to stress to the minister that while I recognize the social insurance number has been used on income tax files since 1966, it is being used more widely so that almost from the day a citizen is born until the day he dies various programs require the social insurance number and it is becoming de facto an identification number. This poses very serious problems in protecting the privacy of citizens, and this parliament enacted legislation on the subject in the last session.
More and more government programs use the social insurance number as a coding number for filing information about individuals, and once it is possible to obtain that social insur-

ance number it is easy to violate privacy and the security surrounding confidential personal information held in government data banks. Mr. Chairman, I should like to reply to the two questions, first to the problem of the religious groups who refuse to have a social insurance number. There is no penalty. They pay the tax when they cash the coupons, and they will get this money back. It is not a penalty. The money is taken as a guarantee that the tax will be paid, and is returned when the tax return is filed. There is no injustice in this.
Like other hon. members, I am concerned because of the incident that came to light on a Toronto radio program where someone found a way to get four different tax returns from different parts of the country. I have had discussions with the Minister of National Revenue and his deputy minister about this. There is a dilemma because very often taxpayers communicate with the department and ask for fast information before making a transaction, and it is possible for them, through the deputy minister perhaps, to get quick information. If we impose an even tighter system, the penalty will be a less responsive system when inquiries are being made.
In light of that, I was extremely preoccupied and impressed by the arguments made by hon. members who have raised this in the House. Every aspect of this affair that I mention today should be investigated by a royal commission. This committee should be delighted to examine this matter in detail. It is not fair that one taxpayer should be treated this way. In a report I have here, Canadian Javelin has admitted paying in excess of $1 million to John C. Doyle, in defiance of a writ of attachment placed on the company in 1965. In a letter to me about a week ago, the Minister of Justice said that he is taking action in the Federal Court-after 12 years of defiance. Only after I repeatedly brought this matter to the attention of the government is he taking action.
This government has permitted John C. Doyle and Canadian Javelin Limited to set up a tax avoidance scheme. Because of this writ of attachment, John C. Doyle set up a company in the Bahamas known as Javelin Export Limited. He owns and controls it. Javelin Export Limited entered into a contract with Canadian Javelin Limited for a ten-year period under which Doyle is to be paid $100,000 per year, tax-free, in the Bahamas. Canadian Javelin Limited is incorporated under federal law, so over $100,000 per year goes to Javelin Export in the Bahamas which pays it over to John C. Doyle who does not pay any Canadian income tax on it. This is open defiance of the laws of Canada, yet the government has done nothing about it.
It is tax avoidance in two ways. He is not paying a cent of tax now, nor in recent years, on the income he receives from Canadian Javelin Limited. It is in defiance, it is an indirect way of getting around this writ of attachment that the government placed with the company in 1965.
[The Deputy Chairma.l
Why has this been allowed to happen? This is what I ask the minister. In fact, this Minister of Finance was minister of national revenue from January, 1968, to July, 1968. He did not do a thing about this for six months. There have been ten ministers of national revenue who have done nothing about this situation. Since 1963 there have been the following: Mr. Garland, Mr. Benson, the present Minister of Finance, Mr. Cote, the hon. member for Windsor West, Mr. Stanbury, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare- and now we have the present minister. We can only hope that the Minister of National Revenue now, the member from Manitoba, will take some action. Ten ministers of national revenue have stood by and done nothing-
Sponged.

-during those years. We have had seven ministers of finance, Walter Gordon, the hon. member for Eglinton, Mr. Benson, Mr. Turner-the sound of their names is enough to turn your stomach-the hon. member for West-mount, the hon. member for Rosedale, and now we have the present Minister of Finance. They have done nothing. They are responsible to the 8,800,000 taxpayers, and they have done nothing. You people opposite don't care. All you want to do is cover it up.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
speechtext: The hon. member should name the ministers of finance and ministers of national revenue between 1956 and 1963.
During the period the hon. member mentions, the Progressive Conservative administration of Canada brought this to the Income Tax Appeal Board and made some progress.
Hear, hear!

And if that government had been re-elected in 1963, this would have been finished by 1965. Here is a gentleman who is going to give you the answer as to why you have been so negligent all those years-it is because of the Liberal politics in Quebec. The minister of federal and provincial affairs should know that. It is because of the Liberal politics in Quebec that this situation has been allowed to occur, Mr. Chairman.
We have also had ministers of justice-Mr. Chevrier, Mr. Favreau, Mr. Mcllraith, Mr. Cardin, and the Prime Minister himself was minister of justice from 1967 to 1968 and he did nothing. He allowed this to continue. He is culpable. He is involved in this negligence, this malfeasance and malfeasance of office-Mr. Turner, the Minister of Transport and the present Minister of Justice who is now taking some action after I have written to him and brought this up in the House on four or five occasions. This is a scandal, Mr. Chairman.

This is a worse scandal than anything that has been suggested with respect to the RCMP or security services. It is far worse. The people of this country have the right to expect that every taxpayer will be treated in a similar manner. But one taxpayer, and a most unsavoury one-just because of his Liberal connections-has been allowed to get away with this for all these years.
Shame.

A typical Grit trick. What is the connection? We get the answer as to why Mr. Doyle is being treated in this singularly favourable manner, this lax manner, this scandalous manner, in the right hon. member for Prince Albert's book, his latest volume, "The Tumultuous Years 1962 to 1967", volume III, at page 192:
Pierre Sevigny has stated that he was approached by John Doyle on election night (Sevigny had been defeated as an Independent in his Montreal riding)-
By the way, it is stated in the book that Mr. Sevigny had received a healthy campaign contribution from John Doyle to run as an independent.
-for the names of any Conservative members who, for an appropriate consideration, might switch to the Liberals. Sevigny, to his credit, refused to be a party to this plan. Thus, Doyle and his associates turned elsewhere.
The facts did not become public until the middle of the 1965 election campaign. On 13 October, 1965, at a press conference in Quebec City, Dr. Guy Marcoux, Social Credit member for Quebec-Montmorency in the last parliament, said that Liberal front-bencher J. W. Pickersgill and mining promoter John Doyle took part in negotiations which led six Social Credit members of Parliament to pledge their support to the Liberal party after the 1963 federal election. He had released that day a 24-page pamphlet entitled "Dans le Meme Sac," in which he described "the affair of the six" as the shadiest usurpation of political power in Canada's history.
Mr. Chairman, this gives us a little hint as to the reason for the tender treatment of Mr. John C. Doyle, because he has been on the grimier fringes of Quebec Liberal politics for many years. In 1963 he took part in convincing six Social Credit MPs in declaring they were not going to support the government, that they would support the Liberal party, so there was a change in government in 1963. That is the suggestion in volume III of "The Tumultuous Years".
There has to be some reason why year after year since 1963, which is 14 years, all this time has passed before these matters were ever brought up and brought to a conclusion in the Supreme Court of Canada. In fact, one of these cases still waits to be heard before the Supreme Court of Canada. Why is it that men of the calibre of the names I have given here today, a lot of able men among them, various ministers of justice, various ministers of national revenue and the various ministers of finance, have allowed that situation to go on since 1963? Surely we cannot assume that the civil servants in the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Justice are that negligent and that slothful. We know that if they have the necessary instructions they will act. They will not be waiting 24 or 27 years to collect income tax owed by anyone. Surely we should have a royal commission to call these ministers and the civil servants before it to find out why, in this case, Mr. John C. Doyle, now a fugitive from justice, now a Panamanian citizen, is allowed to owe this government in
Income Tax
excess of $3.5 million in taxes-and God knows how much more he owes for other tax years.
Why has he never been forced to pay up? Why has he had treatment that no other Canadian taxpayer in the history of Canada has ever had? There should be a royal commission to look into that, and to ask the civil servants which minister instructed them to leave those files alone. Which minister instructed them to allow an appeal to lie dormant before the Supreme Court of Canada for seven years without ever moving it forward. Was it their fault, or did some minister tell them to leave it alone, because ministers had to tell them?
In the normal course of events, these things would have gone on, been heard and disposed of 10 to 15 years ago. Who told them not to get bank guarantees, bonds, sureties or their cash and interest, as everybody else has to do? When the income tax people come slithering in to me, Mr. Chairman, and say that I have to pay up something, you can bet your life I am going to tell them where to go until they show me why they have treated John Christopher Doyle in this manner. There are 8,800,000 Canadian taxpayers out there who are going to get the message: Don't bother paying your taxes, gentlemen. Put in an appeal.
